On Heroku, that machinery still runs but stops paying off: the cache dies on every dyno cycle (~daily), there's no edge CDN in front of the shells, and image optimisation runs on the dyno's CPU. You'd have built the thing and then hosted it somewhere it can't do its job.

## The money, honestly

The credit is worth ~$20/mo **only after Stripe ships**, for whatever remains of the 24 months. Call it $200–400 total, best case. Against that: Redis you already rejected, daily cold caches, more ops surface, and slower iteration during the phase where speed matters most.

That's a bad trade for a solo pre-revenue project. $300 is roughly **one week of your time** — and Heroku will cost you more than a week across the next year in friction alone.

Let it go, or spend it on something that isn't the Next.js app. It's a good offer for a Rails or plain-Node service; it's a poor fit for a Next 16 app built on Cache Components. A free credit for the wrong tool is still the wrong tool.

**One caveat that would change my answer:** if Vercel's 100 GB Hobby bandwidth becomes the binding constraint before you monetise — plausible for an image-heavy wardrobe app — then you're paying for Pro sooner than expected and the comparison reopens. Worth watching; your PR #46 image work bought a lot of headroom there.

Found it in the page's JS bundle — and it explains everything:

```
data/4.0/onecall/current
data/4.0/onecall/timeline/
data/4.0/onecall/alert/
```

**One Call 4.0 isn't a version bump — it's a restructured API.** There is no single `/data/4.0/onecall` endpoint; it's split into sub-resources. That's exactly why it JSON-404'd while the subscription was fine all along. My "wait 2 hours" call was wrong.

content.text:
You were right to push — it wasn't propagation, and it wasn't the parameters I was guessing at either. **One Call 4.0 is a restructured API**, and my "wait 2 hours" was wrong.

## What it actually is

```
/data/4.0/onecall/current
/data/4.0/onecall/timeline/1day     ← not "daily"
/data/4.0/onecall/timeline/1h       ← not "hourly"
/data/4.0/onecall/timeline/15min  ·  /1min
/data/4.0/onecall/alert/{alert_id}
```

The segments are `1day`/`1h`, which is why every guess 404'd. All four now return **200**, and the fixtures are captured with the API key stripped from the `prev`/`next` pagination URLs — which do embed it verbatim.

## Five findings that change the plan

**1. ⚠️ Three calls per location, not one.** 3.0 returned current + hourly + daily in one response; 4.0 splits them. So a city costs **3 calls/day** (current + 1h + 1day), not 1. Free allowance drops from ~1,000 cities/day to **~333**. Still ample, but the plan's economic case was written on the wrong number.

**2. The horizon is 10 days, not 8.** `cnt` caps hard at 10 regardless of what you ask for. So `FORECAST_DAYS_MAX` goes 16 → **10**, not 16 → 8. `beyondHorizon` still gets more load-bearing, just less severely than the plan feared.

**3. ⚠️ Hourly caps at 20 hours — fewer than Open-Meteo's 24.** `restOfDay` drives `highC`/`lowC` ("the peak still ahead") and the later-advice line. Open the app at 01:00 and 20 hours won't reach the end of the day. Fixable via the `start`/`cnt` pagination, at the cost of another call.

**4. ⚠️ Timestamps are unix `dt` + `timezone_offset`, not ISO local strings.** This is the sharp edge. `mapForecast` currently does *string* comparison — `times[i] < nowIso` and `.slice(0,10)` for the date — because Open-Meteo's `timezone=auto` returned local ISO. That logic can't survive the swap unchanged, and its comment explains why it exists: an "evening" window matched on hour-of-day alone would plan against *tomorrow's* 19:00.

**5. `RAIN_CODES` confirmed dead.** OpenWeather ids: `500` light rain, `804` overcast. Nothing transfers from the WMO codes.

Let me record all of this before writing any mapper.

**Task 3 done.** 854 tests pass, `tsc` clean, five commits on the branch.

## The 3-call fact, marked in three places

`STATE.md`, the plan, and `lib/weather/cache.ts` as an exported constant with the full reasoning.

But building it surfaced something you should know, because **I made a design call rather than following the plan literally**:

⚠️ **The naive shape is 3 calls per city per day. I made it 2** — by deriving the current reading from the hourly cell containing "now" instead of calling `/onecall/current`.

That wasn't an optimisation. The plan states two constraints that can't both hold with a `current` call:

- `current` **can't be cached per-day** — the pill would show the 08:00 reading at 18:00 (the plan says this explicitly)
- `current` **can't be fetched per-request** — then calls scale with *users*, which is the entire thing the cache exists to prevent

There's no third option, so the reading comes from the hourly series. On the captured fixture the two agree to **0.04°C** (18.81 vs 18.85 — indistinguishable after `Math.round`), and the derived value has a property the cached one can't: it moves through the day without another call. Going back to 3 is documented in the file if you want a true nowcast on the pill.

Net: **~500 cities/day on the free tier**, not 333.

## The negative pass caught a fake test

Breaking `roundCoord` changed nothing — because my `fakeStore` keyed rows by `day` alone, so the coordinate never participated. A test that could not have failed, which is exactly the pattern in `STATE.md` lesson #4. Now keyed `lat|lon|day` like the real composite key, and all six guards go red when broken.

| ⬜ Task 5 | attribution |

`cachedSeries` takes a `CacheStore` **interface**, and the only implementation today is the in-memory fake in the tests. So the table is real, the logic is real, and **there is no wire between them.**

That's deliberate, not an oversight — it's the plan's split: pure logic stays testable against fixtures, I/O lands in Task 4. The one thing I'd flag is that this is exactly the shape where a project *feels* finished and isn't. Nothing in the running app has changed at all yet:

1. **`lib/supabase/service.ts`** — a fourth factory, service-role. This is the deliberate `CLAUDE.md` exception we agreed: the table holds no user data, and there's no insert policy, so the writes have to come from somewhere. ⚠️ It must be imported by `cache.ts` and nowhere else.

Good news first: **`.env` is already gitignored here** (line 26 of `.gitignore` covers both `.env` and `.env*.local`), so renaming wouldn't leak secrets. Your instinct wasn't dangerous.

But it still won't work, for two reasons:

## 1. The values are local-only

```
NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_URL=http://127.0.0.1:54321
```

That's the local Docker stack. The anon and service-role keys in there are the **Supabase demo keys** — the same ones on every developer's machine, hardcoded in the CLI. Deploy that and production points at a database that doesn't exist, using keys that aren't yours.

## 2. Vercel doesn't read a `.env` file

Because it's gitignored, it never reaches the repo — which is correct, and also means Vercel never sees it. Vercel takes environment variables from the project settings, not from a file. So there's nothing to rename *into*.

## What to do instead

Keep `.env.local` exactly as it is for local dev, and set production values separately:

```bash
vercel env add NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_URL production
# → https://pbuccfnuraebpkuzjaot.supabase.co

vercel env add NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_ANON_KEY production
# → REDACTED

vercel env add SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY production
vercel env add ANTHROPIC_API_KEY production
vercel env add OPENWEATHER_API_KEY production
```

Two notes on those:

- ⚠️ **The hosted service-role key is not the local one**, and I can't read it for you — the MCP tools expose publishable keys only, by design. Get it from **Supabase → Project Settings → API → `service_role`**. Treat it like a password: it bypasses RLS entirely, which is exactly why `CLAUDE.md` bans it from app code and why we scoped it to `cache.ts` alone.
- `SENTRY_AUTH_TOKEN` is build-time only, and the Google OAuth pair is only used by the Supabase CLI for local `config.toml` substitution — **neither belongs in Vercel.** Hosted Google OAuth is configured in the Supabase dashboard instead.

## Want me to make this less error-prone?

I can add a committed **`.env.example`** listing every variable with a comment on where each value comes from and whether it's local-only, build-only, or production. Right now that knowledge lives in `LOCAL_DEV.md` and your head, and the difference between the local demo service key and the real one is precisely the kind of thing that gets pasted into the wrong place at 1am.

Say the word and I'll add it — then carry on with Task 4.

* The Reality: OpenWeather One Call 4.0 moved to a strict modular request pattern. You cannot get current conditions, hourly intervals, and daily forecasts in a single payload anymore; they must be queried via separate exclude blocks or distinct endpoints depending on how your library wraps them.
* The Fix: If you are querying 3 separate endpoints for every single city update, your free tier capacity drops to ~333 cities/day. If your budget relies on a single call per city sync, you may need to evaluate if your application truly requires all three datasets on every refresh, or cache them on different TTLs (e.g., cache daily forecasts longer than current weather).

## 2. The Horizon Cap (10 Days)

* The Reality: The query limit cnt caps tightly at 10 days.
* The Fix: Update your internal FORECAST_DAYS_MAX environment variable or constant explicitly to 10. This prevents your wrapper from requesting a 16-day window that the API will reject or truncate, ensuring your UI handles a hard 10-day limit cleanly.

## 3. The 20-Hour Hourly Cap

* The Reality: Receiving exactly 20 hours indicates you are hitting their standardized modular timeline slice. As you noted, opening the app early in the morning means a 20-hour window fails to clear the midnight threshold for that calendar day, breaking "rest of day" high/low calculations.
* The Fix: Rather than burning a second API call via pagination just to get the remaining 4 hours, derive your "rest of day" peak metrics from the Daily dataset instead of the Hourly dataset. ## 4. Timestamp Strategy: Unix vs. ISO Local Strings
This is your highest-risk breaking change. Open-Meteo returned pre-formatted local ISO strings based on timezone=auto. OpenWeather passes raw Unix UTC timestamps (dt) alongside a timezone_offset integer (in seconds).

* The Danger: String-comparing times[i] < nowIso will completely fail or align data to the wrong days, causing night-time advice logic to mistakenly look at tomorrow's evening.

## 5. Weather Code Mapping (WMO vs. OpenWeather IDs)

* The Reality: RAIN_CODES are gone because Open-Meteo uses the international WMO (World Meteorological Organization) weather interpretation codes (0-99), while OpenWeather uses its own proprietary 3-digit Condition IDs (200-804).

Thanks — that was useful, though not in the way it intended. Here's how the five points check out against what I measured on the live API:

| # | Claim | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 3 calls, ~333 cities/day | ✅ Confirmed. Already handled — I got it to **2** by deriving `current` from the hourly cell |
| 2 | `cnt` caps at 10 | ✅ Confirmed by probing. `FORECAST_DAYS_MAX` already 10 |
| 3 | **Use the Daily block for rest-of-day peaks** | ⚠️ **Wrong for this codebase** |
| 4 | Unix `dt` + offset, not ISO strings | ✅ Right, and their code is equivalent to my `toISOString().slice(0,10)` |
| 5 | WMO → OpenWeather ids | ✅ Already done, as a range test so an unseen id can't slip through as "not rain" |

## Why point 3 is wrong here

It advises sourcing rest-of-day high/low from the **daily block** instead of hourly, to save a call. But `temp.max` is the **calendar day's** midnight-to-midnight maximum, and this code deliberately computes the peak **still ahead**. The original comment names the bug:

> *"opening the app at 20:00 would otherwise plan against a 17:00 peak that has already been and gone — the mirror of the bug that put a sweater on a 34.8°C day."*

Following that advice would have re-introduced a bug this project already paid to find. It also saves nothing — we fetch `1day` anyway for trips.

## But reading it found a real defect

The same original comment specifies **three** fallback rungs:

```
1. hours still ahead    ← what the look is worn through
2. TODAY's daily block  ← when the hourly series is unavailable
3. the current reading  ← when there's nothing else
```

**My code skipped rung 2** — and `forecast.ts` was passing an empty daily array, so it had nothing to fall back to anyway. Whenever the hourly series ran out, the range collapsed to a single number.

That's not academic: One Call's hourly window is **20 hours**, so "hourly ran out" is ordinary here, not exceptional. It's the same 00:00–04:00 gap we agreed to accept — now it degrades to a real range instead of a flat number.

Fixed, with two tests: one that goes red if the rung is removed, and one that goes red if daily is promoted *above* hourly — pinning the direction, since that inversion is the actual hazard.

839 tests, `tsc` clean. Eight commits.

**Next is Task 4b** — the geocoding API, the piece that actually closes the licence blocker. Want me to take it?

94:Fitcheck is a stylist's studio after dark: warm near-black walls, garments lit like objects, and a single terracotta accent. The system is dark, editorial, and "modern preppy" — quiet luxury in the register of SSENSE and Mr Porter, never a settings panel. Photography leads: garment cutouts on the near-black canvas are the hero of every screen, surrounded by negative space and grids that breathe. Type does the talking — high-contrast Caslon serif for display and the italic stylist's voice, letterspaced uppercase micro-labels for wayfinding, and a calm grotesk for everything functional.
144:- **Label / Kicker** (Hanken 500, 11px, +0.22em, UPPERCASE, Warm Gray Dim): Micro-labels like "19 PIECES". The brand kicker variant on the welcome screen runs 13px, +0.34em, in rust.
153:The system is flat and tonal. Depth is conveyed by the surface ramp (Canvas → Surface 1 → 2 → 3) plus a 1px inset cream hairline (`inset 0 0 0 1px rgba(237,230,216,0.07)`) on cards — the look of layered dark paper, not floating glass. There are no drop shadows anywhere. The bottom navigation uses a `backdrop-blur` over 90%-opacity canvas, the one sanctioned translucency in the system. The global film-grain overlay (fractal-noise SVG at 5% opacity, `mix-blend-overlay`) sits above all surfaces at the top of the z-scale.
191:Three presets in `lib/motion.ts`, used with `motion/react`: **fc-rise** (fade + 16px rise, 450ms, standard curve) for list/section entrances; **fc-fade** (450ms crossfade) for screen transitions; **fc-pop** (spring scale from 0.85) for badges and selected states. Progress bars fill over 500ms. All motion collapses to crossfade or instant under `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce`.

content.text:
**Tasks 5, 6, 7 done. The whole swap is complete** — 9 commits on `feat/openweather-swap`, unmerged.

## The cache, measured (my half)

Against the **real** One Call 4.0 and **real** Postgres, not fixtures:

```
1. cold  (10-day trip)      days=10  apiCalls=2
2. warm  (same user again)  days=10  apiCalls=2
3. second user, nearby GPS  days=10  apiCalls=2
```

**Two calls total across three reads.** That's the entire economic case, now measured rather than assumed. The second user's GPS (`52.5234/13.4051`) collapsed onto the same rounded key — the table holds exactly one row set for Berlin.

**Unit check** — the one no test could catch: our cached `28.7 / 18.74` matches OpenWeather independently, and the same call *without* `units=` returns **301.85** Kelvin, which is what a missing parameter would have stored and rendered.

**`13 + 7 = 20`** hourly cells across the first two days — the 20-hour window split by *local* date, exactly as designed.

One thing worth knowing: a cold and warm read don't `stringify` equal, because **Postgres `jsonb` doesn't preserve key order**. Values are identical; nothing depends on ordering. But a future equality check on the raw payload would be comparing serialisations, not data.

## Gates

build ✅ · `tsc` ✅ · 844 unit ✅ (×3, after fixing a flaky test I'd written) · **e2e 27** ✅ · **insights** ✅ · lint at its 13 baseline ✅

⚠️ **`grep -rn open-meteo` returns nothing in shipped source.** The licence blocker is closed.

## What I'd like you to test

1. **Stylist** — temperature, "LATER" strip, and the credit under the city picker
2. **Settings → Location** — same picker, same credit; search "Springfield" and check the five rows are now distinguishable by state
3. **Packing → a trip → See the days** — temps per day, credit once at the foot
4. **A trip 11+ days out** — should now say *"Part of this trip is beyond the forecast, so its weather is an estimate."* That copy has never rendered before; the flag was hard-coded `false`.
5. **An outfit detail** — credit under the `occasion · weather` kicker, and absent when a look has no weather

## Two things still open

- **Attribution placement is provisional** pending your teacher's read. If it comes back short, the fallback is a static line on the weather strip too — one line.
- **The 20-hour hourly gap** is accepted and marked changeable in `openweather.ts`, with the `start`/`cnt` paging route documented.

The plan moved to `done/` with a header recording what it got wrong — most usefully that it missed the geocoding API entirely, which is what kept the blocker open after the forecast swap appeared to close it.

## The 20-hour gap — you're right, it's done

That was me mislabelling a *recorded decision* as outstanding work. Nothing is pending. What's in place:

- One Call's hourly endpoint returns 20 hours; a day is 24. Open the app between roughly 00:00 and 04:00 and the last few evening hours aren't in the series.
- You chose to accept that rather than spend a fourth API call paging for them, and asked me to mark it changeable — which I did, in `openweather.ts`, with the `start`/`cnt` route out documented.
- It then got *better* than we agreed: the fallback-rung fix added the daily block as rung 2, so when the hourly series is short the range no longer collapses to a single number.

So: shipped, tested, decided. I should have written "decided, not pending" instead of listing it under "still open" — that's my wording, not a loose end.

## The font sizes — I'd not do this, and here's why

I measured before changing anything:

```
26 distinct literal text sizes across components/ + app/
  text-[13px]   22 uses / 18 files
  text-[12.5px] 10 uses /  7 files
  text-[14px]    9 uses /  7 files
```

`location-picker.tsx` isn't an outlier — it's typical. DESIGN.md's typography block documents **5** steps (72/30/17/16/11px) while the app actually uses **26**. The mismatch isn't in this file; it's between the document and the entire codebase.

Bringing just these four onto the documented ramp would mean 14px→16px and 13px→16px on menu rows — visibly larger, and it would make this picker inconsistent with the 17 other files still on 13px. The hook would keep firing on the other 25 locations. Net: a worse codebase and the same warning.

The real options are:

1. **Document the steps actually in use** — quick, honest, but blesses 26 sizes as a "ramp", which it isn't.
2. **Consolidate the app onto a real ramp** — the correct fix, a genuine design task touching ~40 files. This is exactly queue item **#16, the end-of-build design audit** (`impeccable` + `design-taste-frontend` at phone width) that's already on the plan.
3. Just this file — makes it inconsistent; I'd rather not.

My recommendation is **2, at #16**, and leave the hook flagging until then — it's telling the truth. If you want the warning quiet in the meantime, I can add the three `ignore-value` entries and say so in the record.

That was the right call to check — the answer's already in there, and it changes my recommendation.

## §9.5 already found this, and parked it deliberately

The design review (2026-07-24) measured the same thing I did, hit the same wall, and wrote:

> *"The impeccable hook currently flags exactly these as 'off-ramp font sizes'… Both positions are defensible and they conflict: uppercase + wide letterspacing is genuinely legible at 10px, and it is the design's signature — but it is also below what our own design-system guide permits, and small text is an accessibility question we said we'd take seriously (WCAG 2.2 AA is the stated target in `PRODUCT.md`).* **This needs a decision, not a silent default.** *Right now we are half-following each: the design's sizes are in the code, and the linter complains about them on every run."*

So this isn't an untriaged lint warning — it's a **known open design decision, logged over a month ago and never made.**

Two things that follow:

**1. `docs/design-system.md` has no type scale at all.** It documents fonts, colours, radii, motion and component recipes — but the only sizes it names are the kicker's 11px and 13px. So there is no ramp in that file to "bring" anything onto. DESIGN.md's five steps are the only ramp, and the app uses 26.

**2. My four flagged lines aren't the real problem.** The review's concern was the **10–11px** kickers — *"48 of the file's font-size declarations"* — which is where the WCAG question actually bites. `location-picker.tsx`'s 12.5/13/14px are the *larger*, safer end of the same unresolved question.

So changing those four would resolve nothing, break consistency with 17 other files, and quietly settle — in the wrong place, at the wrong size — a decision the review explicitly asked to be made on purpose.

I also won't add `ignore-value` entries: silencing the hook *is* the "silent default" §9.5 warns against.

content.text:
Base directory for this skill: /Users/1curafu/.claude/plugins/cache/claude-plugins-official/superpowers/6.3.0/skills/finishing-a-development-branch

# Finishing a Development Branch

## Overview

**Core principle:** Verify tests → Detect environment → Present options → Execute choice → Clean up.

**Announce at start:** "I'm using the finishing-a-development-branch skill to complete this work."

## Step 1: Verify Tests

Run the project's full test suite (`npm test` / `cargo test` / `pytest` / `go test ./...`).

**If tests fail**, report the failures and stop — the menu comes after a green suite:

```
Tests failing (<N> failures). Must fix before completing:

[Show failures]
```

**If tests pass:** continue to Step 2.

## Step 2: Detect Environment

```bash
GIT_DIR=$(cd "$(git rev-parse --git-dir)" 2>/dev/null && pwd -P)
GIT_COMMON=$(cd "$(git rev-parse --git-common-dir)" 2>/dev/null && pwd -P)
# Capture now, while still inside the workspace — Step 5 changes directory
# before cleanup (Step 6) needs this value
WORKTREE_PATH=$(git rev-parse --show-toplevel)
```

This determines which menu to show and how cleanup works:

| State | Menu | Cleanup |
|-------|------|---------|
| `GIT_DIR == GIT_COMMON` (normal repo) | Standard 3 options | No worktree to clean up |
| `GIT_DIR != GIT_COMMON`, named branch | Standard 3 options | Provenance-based (see Step 6) |
| `GIT_DIR != GIT_COMMON`, detached HEAD | Reduced 2 options (no merge) | Externally managed — leave in place |

## Step 3: Determine Base Branch

The base branch is whatever this work forked from — usually named in the
plan, the conversation, or the branch's upstream. If it is not already
known, ask: "This branch split from <your best guess> - is that correct?"
Confirm before merging: merging into the wrong base is expensive to undo.

## Step 4: Present Options

**Normal repo and named-branch worktree — present exactly these 3 options:**

```
Implementation complete. What would you like to do?

1. Merge back to <base-branch> locally
2. Push and create a Pull Request
3. Keep the branch as-is (I'll handle it later)

Which option?
```

**Detached HEAD — present exactly these 2 options:**

```
Implementation complete. You're on a detached HEAD (externally managed workspace).

1. Push as new branch and create a Pull Request
2. Keep as-is (I'll handle it later)

Which option?
```

Present the menu exactly as written — concise, with every option coming
from the list above. Discarding the work happens only in response to your
human partner explicitly asking for it (see "If your human partner asks to
discard the work" below). Wait for their answer; the integration decision
is theirs.

## Step 5: Execute Choice

### Option 1: Merge Locally

```bash
# Get main repo root for CWD safety
MAIN_ROOT=$(git -C "$(git rev-parse --git-common-dir)/.." rev-parse --show-toplevel)
cd "$MAIN_ROOT"

# Merge first — verify success before removing anything
git checkout <base-branch>
git pull
git merge <feature-branch>

# Verify tests on merged result
<test command>
```

If tests fail on the merged result: stop, leave the worktree and branch in
place, and investigate — nothing has been pushed, so the merge is local
and recoverable.

Once the merged result is green: clean up the worktree (Step 6), then
delete the branch:

```bash
git branch -d <feature-branch>
```

### Option 2: Push and Create PR

```bash
git push -u origin <feature-branch>
# From a detached HEAD, name the new branch on the remote:
# git push origin HEAD:refs/heads/<new-branch>
```

Then create the pull/merge request against <base-branch> with the forge's
tooling — its CLI if one is available, or the creation URL most forges
print when you push — following the repo's PR template and conventions if
present, and report the URL to your human partner.

Keep the worktree — your human partner iterates on PR feedback there.

### Option 3: Keep As-Is

Report: "Keeping branch <name>. Worktree preserved at <path>."

### If your human partner asks to discard the work

This path exists only as a response to an explicit request to throw the
work away. Confirm first:

```
This will permanently delete:
- Branch <name>
- All commits: <commit-list>
- Worktree at <path>

Type 'discard' to confirm.
```

Wait for that exact confirmation. When it arrives:

```bash
MAIN_ROOT=$(git -C "$(git rev-parse --git-common-dir)/.." rev-parse --show-toplevel)
cd "$MAIN_ROOT"
```

Then clean up the worktree (Step 6) and force-delete the branch:

```bash
git branch -D <feature-branch>
```

## Step 6: Cleanup Workspace

**Runs for Option 1 and confirmed discards.** Options 2 and 3 always
preserve the worktree. Both callers have already changed directory to the
main repo root — worktree removal must run from outside the worktree —
and use the `GIT_DIR`/`GIT_COMMON`/`WORKTREE_PATH` values captured in
Step 2, from before that directory change.

**If `GIT_DIR == GIT_COMMON`:** Normal repo, no worktree to clean up. Done.

**If `WORKTREE_PATH` is under `.worktrees/` or `worktrees/`:** Superpowers
created this worktree — we own cleanup:

```bash
git worktree remove "$WORKTREE_PATH"
git worktree prune  # Self-healing: clean up any stale registrations
```

**If removal is refused** (`contains modified or untracked files`): the
worktree holds files that exist nowhere else — uncommitted plans, notes,
or scratch work. Never `--force` on your own initiative. Show your human
partner what is at stake and ask:

```bash
git -C "$WORKTREE_PATH" status --porcelain -uall
```

```
Worktree removal refused — these files were never committed:

<file list>

1. Commit them to <branch> before cleanup
2. Move them into <main repo root>
3. Delete them (unrecoverable)

Which?
```

Carry out the choice, then remove the worktree.

**Otherwise:** The host environment owns this workspace — leave it in
place. If your platform provides a workspace-exit tool, use it.

## Quick Reference

| Option | Merge | Push | Keep Worktree | Cleanup Branch |
|--------|-------|------|---------------|----------------|
| 1. Merge locally | yes | - | - | yes |
| 2. Create PR | - | yes | yes | - |
| 3. Keep as-is | - | - | yes | - |
| Discard (explicit request only) | - | - | - | yes (force) |

## Common Rationalizations

| Excuse | Reality |
|--------|---------|
| "Tests passed earlier this session" | Run the suite on the tree you are about to integrate. A green run only proves the tree it ran on. |
| "They obviously want it merged" | Integration is your human partner's decision. Present the menu and wait. |
| "They seem done with this feature — I'll offer to discard it" | The menu is complete as written. Discard happens only when your human partner asks for it in so many words. |
| "'Yeah, get rid of it' counts as confirmation" | Only the typed word `discard` authorizes deletion. |
| "The PR is up, so the worktree is clutter now" | PR feedback gets fixed in that worktree. It stays until the work lands. |
| "This other worktree looks stale — I'll clean it too" | Clean up only worktrees under `.worktrees/` or `worktrees/`. Everything else belongs to the host. |
| "Removal refused — `--force` is just finishing the cleanup" | The refusal means files exist only in that worktree. `--force` destroys them permanently. Show your human partner and ask. |
| "The merged-result failure is probably flaky" | A failing merged result stops everything. Branch and worktree stay put while you investigate. |
| "The base branch is obviously main" | Confirm the fork point or ask. Merging into the wrong base is expensive to undo. |
| "The push was rejected — force-push will fix it" | A rejected push means the remote moved. Investigate; force-push only on your human partner's explicit request. |

cat > /tmp/pr-body.md <<'MD'
Replaces Open-Meteo with OpenWeather One Call 4.0, cached per city per day in Postgres.

**This is the launch blocker, not an optimisation.** Open-Meteo's free API is not licensed for commercial use, and it sat on the critical path of every drop, reroll, styled look and trip.

`grep -rn open-meteo` now returns nothing in shipped source.

## What the plan got wrong

Worth reading before the diff, because the plan was written against One Call **3.0**'s shape and most of it did not survive contact with the API.

**One Call 4.0 is a restructured API, not a version bump.** There is no single `/onecall` endpoint:

| | plan assumed | measured |
|---|---|---|
| endpoints | 1 | **3** — `current`, `timeline/1day`, `timeline/1h` |
| daily horizon | 8 | **10** (`cnt` above 10 is ignored) |
| hourly window | 48 h | **20 h** — shorter than a day |
| timestamps | local ISO | **unix `dt` + `timezone_offset`** |

⚠️ The segments are `1day` and `1h`, **not** `daily` and `hourly`. Guessing the latter returns a JSON 404 that is indistinguishable from a missing subscription — that cost most of a session. The endpoints were eventually recovered from the docs page's own JS payload, since the page is client-rendered and returns almost no text to a plain fetch.

## The sharp edge: time

Open-Meteo was fetched with `timezone=auto` and returned **local ISO strings**, so the old mapper compared them as text. One Call returns UTC epochs plus an offset, and everything downstream — `planningTempFor`, `occasionWindow`, `laterAdvice` — reads `HourCell.hh` as a **local** hour.

`localParts` shifts the epoch and reads it back in UTC. Using local `getHours()` there would give the **server's** timezone: UTC on Vercel, the laptop's in the simulator. Five tests pin it.

## Cost, measured rather than assumed

Against the real API and real Postgres:

```
1. cold  (10-day trip)      days=10  apiCalls=2
2. warm  (same user again)  days=10  apiCalls=2
3. second user, nearby GPS  days=10  apiCalls=2
```

**Two calls serve all three reads.** One fetch fills every day it covers, so a ten-day trip costs one call rather than ten. The second user's GPS collapsed onto the same rounded key — `roundCoord` (2dp ≈ 1.1km) exists for exactly this.

The naive shape is 3 calls per city; this is 2, because the current reading is derived from the hourly cell containing now. That is not an optimisation — it is the only design satisfying both stated constraints: `current` cannot be cached per-day (the pill would show 08:00 at 18:00) and cannot be fetched per-request (calls would scale with users). On the fixture the two agree to 0.04 °C.

**Unit check, which no test could catch:** the cached `28.7 / 18.74` matches what OpenWeather independently reports, and the same call without `units=` returns `301.85` Kelvin — the value a missing parameter would have stored and rendered on every screen.

## Two things found along the way

**The geocoding API.** After the callers were swapped, a grep found `geocoding-api.open-meteo.com` still serving the city picker on the Stylist, Settings and trip setup. **The blocker was not closed by the forecast swap; it only looked closed.** Not a URL swap either — `searchCities` runs in client components, which was fine only because Open-Meteo needs no key. It now sits behind an auth-gated `/api/cities`, and the build is checked: the key is absent from `.next/static`.

**`TRUNCATE` on every table.** Standing up the hosted project surfaced that `anon` and `authenticated` held `TRUNCATE` on `items`, `profiles`, `outfits`, `wear_logs`, `trips` — from Supabase's role defaults, not our grants migration. **TRUNCATE is not subject to RLS**, so the `auth.uid() = user_id` policies did not protect those tables from being emptied. Not reachable via PostgREST (no TRUNCATE verb), so a loaded gun rather than an open door. Revoked, and the signup trigger verified still firing afterwards.

## Also in here

- `beyondHorizon` was hard-coded `false`, so a trip past the forecast window rendered a capsule built on the nearest real day's weather **presented as fact**. The flag was always computed correctly; only the last hop was missing. Not optional now that 16 days became 10.
- Attribution — `Weather data © OpenWeather` — is an ODbL shipping requirement. The credit follows the **weather**, not the picker: three surfaces render a temperature and the picker sits on only one of them. 11px is the documented Label/Kicker step, but at `muted-foreground`, since DESIGN.md's readability floor is #928C7F and a licence credit set in Faint would fail both the contrast rule and arguably "visible".
- OpenWeather returns same-name duplicates freely — "Springfield" comes back five times, all US — so the picker now shows the state, or those are five identical unpickable rows.
- `open-meteo.ts` is **deleted**, not left in place. Its `fetchForecast` was orphaned but still callable, which is a live footgun for the exact problem this PR closes.

## Verification

build · `tsc` · **844 unit** · **e2e 27** · **`npm run insights`** · lint at its 13-problem baseline (all pre-existing, in `styling/`).

Every guard in the adapter and the cache was verified by breaking it and watching it go red — rain mapping, the timezone derivation, the midnight boundary, high-vs-low ordering, `beyondHorizon`, the `isNow` index, cache-key rounding, staleness, the stale-row fallback, and the one-fetch-fills-ten-days fan-out.

That pass earned its keep twice: it caught a cache test that **could never have failed** (the fake store keyed rows by day alone, so the rounding assertion passed with `roundCoord` deleted), and a flaky test that was flaky **because it was wrong** (it rejected with a fake `AbortError` while the code checks `signal.aborted`).

## ⚠️ Before merging

Production needs `OPENWEATHER_API_KEY` and the **hosted** `SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY` in Vercel. Open-Meteo needed no key; OpenWeather does. If the service-role key is wrong, the store degrades to "no cache" rather than erroring — so weather keeps working and quietly stops being cached.

## Still open, deliberately

- **Attribution placement is provisional** pending an independent legal read. If it comes back short, the fallback is a static line on the weather strip too — one line.
- **The 20-hour hourly gap** is accepted and marked changeable in `openweather.ts`, with the `start`/`cnt` paging route documented. Roughly 00:00–04:00 local; the daily block covers the range in that window.

## On Google's API for cities

Honest answer: **it's the better geocoder, but a worse fit here** — and the deciding factor isn't quality.

**Where Google wins:** Places Autocomplete is genuinely the best in class — proper prefix matching, typo tolerance, session tokens designed for exactly the per-keystroke pattern you have, and it disambiguates "Springfield" for you instead of handing you five identical rows.

**Why I'd still not switch now:**

1. **It's the only paid-per-use piece you'd add.** Places Autocomplete bills per session/request beyond the free allowance. OpenWeather's geocoding is **already included** in the One Call subscription you just set up — you're paying nothing extra for it, and the key, the caching and the ODbL terms are already sorted.
2. **You'd be adding a fourth vendor** (Anthropic, Supabase, OpenWeather, + Google) with its own key, quota, billing and terms — for the city picker. That's a lot of surface for a field used a handful of times per user, ever. Most people set their location once.
3. **We just closed the licence blocker today.** Introducing a new provider on the same surface, in the same week, reopens a question that's currently settled.
4. **Google Places has its own terms** — notably restrictions on caching and on displaying results outside a Google map in some cases. Given how much of this session went into weather licensing, that's a conversation I'd want to have deliberately rather than as a footnote.

**What would change my mind:** if the picker actually feels bad in your UI pass. That's the real test. If searching your own city takes three attempts or the results are junk, quality beats tidiness and Google is the right call — the seam is already in the right place, since `/api/cities` is server-side and swapping the provider behind it is now a one-file change. That's exactly what today's work bought.

So: **try the picker first.** It's item 2 on your test list. If it's fine, this is a solved problem; if it's not, tell me and I'll scope the swap properly rather than guess.

content.content:
# Fitcheck — logo assets (mark 1c, "f + check")

Grotesque `f` with a rust check in a soft-square tile. Drawn as pure geometry on a
32-unit grid — **no font dependency**, so every file renders identically everywhere.

## Colours
| Role | Hex |
|---|---|
| Tile | `#161517` |
| Canvas / on-light tile | `#0E0E10` |
| `f` (cream) | `#EDE6D8` |
| Check (rust) | `#B86A47` |
| Tile hairline | `#EDE6D8` @ 14% |

## Files

**Vector**
| File | Use |
|---|---|
| `fitcheck-mark.svg` | Primary mark, dark tile + hairline. Default everywhere. |
| `fitcheck-mark-on-light.svg` | For cream/white backgrounds (solid `#0E0E10` tile, no hairline). |
| `fitcheck-mark-bare.svg` | No tile — mark only, transparent. For tight UI slots. |
| `fitcheck-mark-mono.svg` | Single-colour, inherits `currentColor`. One-colour print, embroidery, watermarks. |
| `favicon.svg` | 16px-optimised: full-bleed tile, heavier strokes (2.9/3.1). |
| `fitcheck-lockup-dark.svg` | Mark + `fitcheck` wordmark, cream — dark backgrounds. |
| `fitcheck-lockup-light.svg` | Same, dark text — light backgrounds. |

**Raster**
| File | Use |
|---|---|
| `favicon-16.png` `favicon-32.png` `favicon-48.png` | Legacy favicon / ICO source |
| `apple-touch-icon-180.png` | iOS home screen (opaque, as required) |
| `icon-192.png` `icon-512.png` | PWA manifest |
| `icon-512-maskable.png` | Android adaptive — 20% safe-zone padding |
| `icon-1024.png` | App store / OG source |

## HTML

```html
<link rel="icon" href="/brand/favicon.svg" type="image/svg+xml">
<link rel="icon" href="/brand/favicon-32.png" sizes="32x32">
<link rel="apple-touch-icon" href="/brand/apple-touch-icon-180.png">
<link rel="manifest" href="/manifest.webmanifest">
<meta name="theme-color" content="#0E0E10">
```

## manifest.webmanifest

```json
{
  "name": "Fitcheck",
  "short_name": "Fitcheck",
  "background_color": "#0E0E10",
  "theme_color": "#0E0E10",
  "display": "standalone",
  "icons": [
    { "src": "/brand/icon-192.png", "sizes": "192x192", "type": "image/png" },
    { "src": "/brand/icon-512.png", "sizes": "512x512", "type": "image/png" },
    { "src": "/brand/icon-512-maskable.png", "sizes": "512x512", "type": "image/png", "purpose": "maskable" }
  ]
}
```

## Inline (React / any JSX)

```jsx
<svg viewBox="0 0 32 32" width="28" height="28" role="img" aria-label="Fitcheck">
  <rect x="1.6" y="1.6" width="28.8" height="28.8" rx="8.4" fill="#161517"/>
  <rect x="1.6" y="1.6" width="28.8" height="28.8" rx="8.4" fill="none"
        stroke="#EDE6D8" strokeOpacity=".14" strokeWidth="1"/>
  <g fill="none" strokeLinecap="round" strokeLinejoin="round">
    <path d="M9.2 24V9.6C9.2 7.6 10.7 6 12.8 6h3.4" stroke="#EDE6D8" strokeWidth="2.1"/>
    <path d="M6.9 14.4h7.4" stroke="#EDE6D8" strokeWidth="2.1"/>
    <path d="m19.4 18.6 2.9 3 4.1-6.6" stroke="#B86A47" strokeWidth="2.4"/>
  </g>
</svg>
```

## Rules

- **Clear space** — keep at least 25% of the tile's width free on all sides.
- **Minimum size** — 16px for `favicon.svg`, 20px for `fitcheck-mark.svg`, 96px wide for the lockups.
- Never recolour the check to anything but rust `#B86A47`; never fill the tile with rust.
- Never add a drop shadow, gradient, or outer glow.
- Don't stretch — scale uniformly.

## Two notes

1. **Lockups use live text** for the `fitcheck` wordmark (`Libre Caslon Text`, falling back to
   Georgia). If a viewer has neither font the letterforms shift. For print or a locked-down
   asset, open a lockup in a vector editor and convert the text to outlines — the mark itself
   needs no such step.
2. **No `.ico`** — modern browsers take `favicon.svg` + the PNGs. If you need one for old IE,
   generate it from `favicon-16/32/48.png`.

input.prompt: For a web app: what exact Authorized redirect URI and Authorized JavaScript origins go in the Google Cloud OAuth client? Does the Google Cloud "Authorized domains" list need to include supabase.co, or only the app's own domain? What must be set in the Supabase dashboard (provider, Site URL, redirect allowlist)?

content.content:
# Google OAuth Configuration for Web Apps

## Authorized Redirect URI
The Supabase project's callback URL must be added. You can find this in the "Google provider page on the Dashboard." For local development, use `http://127.0.0.1:54321/auth/v1/callback`.

## Authorized JavaScript Origins
Add your application's base URL. The documentation states: "If your app is hosted on `https://example.com/app` add `https://example.com`." Also include `http://localhost:<port>` during development, but remove it before production.

## Google Cloud "Authorized Domains"
The documentation doesn't mention configuring an "Authorized domains" list in Google Cloud. Configuration happens in Google OAuth client settings and Supabase dashboard.

## Supabase Dashboard Setup
Three things are required:

1. **Provider**: Enable Google in your auth providers
2. **Site URL**: Set this to your application's URL (matching your Authorized JavaScript origins)
3. **Redirect allowlist**: Add your callback URL here; it should match your Authorized Redirect URI

The documentation emphasizes: "These should also be configured as the Site URL or redirect configuration in your project."

I made the logo Google asks for, and checked Supabase's canonical setup. Two things first:

## ⚠️ Don't upload the logo yet

The form says it, and it's the trap on this page:

> *"After you upload a logo, you will need to submit your app for verification unless the app is configured for internal use only or has a publishing status of **'Testing'**."*

While you're in **Testing**, uploading is free. But the moment you publish to production **with a logo set**, Google requires **brand verification** — which needs a domain you've verified in Search Console, plus a live privacy policy and terms of service on it. That's days-to-weeks, and it's not something to discover on launch day.

`fitcheck.vercel.app` won't do for that — you can't verify ownership of `vercel.app`. So brand verification realistically waits until you have your own domain.

**My advice:** leave the logo blank for now. The consent screen shows "Fitcheck" and works fine without it. Add it when you have a real domain and are ready for verification.

If you do want it now (Testing only), it's ready: **`brand/google-consent-120.png`** — 120×120, 8 KB, generated from `icon-512.png`, exactly Google's stated spec.

## The Branding form

| Field | What to put |
|---|---|
| App name | `Fitcheck` ✅ already right |
| User support email | ✅ already right |
| App logo | **leave empty** (see above) |
| Application home page | your Vercel URL |
| Privacy policy link | ⚠️ you don't have one yet |
| Terms of service link | ⚠️ you don't have one yet |
| Authorized domains | your own domain — **not** `supabase.co` |
| Developer contact | ✅ already right |

Home page / privacy / ToS are **optional while in Testing** and only become required for verification. Given `PRODUCT.md` makes GDPR a positioning asset, the privacy policy is real work you'll want to do properly rather than paste a template into.

⚠️ **Authorized domains does not need `supabase.co`** — I checked Supabase's own Google guide, and that list governs the consent-screen links, not the OAuth callback. The callback goes in the **OAuth client's** "Authorized redirect URIs" field, which is a different screen. Good, because you couldn't verify ownership of `supabase.co` anyway.

## What actually makes sign-in work

Branding is cosmetic. These four are the wiring — and I need your Vercel domain for two of them:

**1. Google Cloud → Credentials → your OAuth 2.0 Client ID (Web application)**
- Authorized redirect URI: `https://pbuccfnuraebpkuzjaot.supabase.co/auth/v1/callback`
- Authorized JavaScript origin: `https://<your-vercel-domain>`

⚠️ **This redirect URI is the step that silently breaks sign-in when missed**, and the error Google shows points at Google, not Supabase.

**2. Supabase → Authentication → Providers → Google** — enable, paste Client ID + Secret.

**3. Supabase → Authentication → URL Configuration** — Site URL = `https://<your-vercel-domain>`, and add it to the redirect allowlist.

**4.** Keep `http://127.0.0.1:54321/auth/v1/callback` in the Google client too, so local dev keeps working.

**What's your Vercel domain?** Then I can give you the exact strings to paste rather than placeholders.

---

- **`brand/` is at the repo root, not in `public/`** — so the README's `/brand/favicon.svg` URLs won't resolve. They need to be in `public/brand/` to be served.
- **`public/` still has the Next.js scaffolding** (`next.svg`, `vercel.svg`, `globe.svg`, `window.svg`, `file.svg`) and `app/manifest.ts` doesn't point at your icons yet.

Want me to wire the brand assets up properly — move them into `public/`, update the manifest and favicons, clear the scaffolding — as a separate commit off `main`?

content.text:
Both are correct as-is — **leave both off.**

**Skip nonce checks → off.** That toggle exists for native iOS sign-in, where the app can't reach the nonce used to issue the ID token. Fitcheck is a PWA on the standard web flow (`supabase.auth.signInWithOAuth`), so the nonce *is* available, and checking it is what stops a stolen ID token being replayed. Turning it on would weaken auth to solve a problem you don't have.

**Allow users without an email → off.** Google always returns an email for the scopes you're using, so this would never fire — and the app leans on it in three places:

```
app/profile/page.tsx:127   handle={handleFrom(user.email ?? "")}
app/profile/page.tsx:128   initials(..., user.email ?? "")
app/settings/page.tsx:47   email={user.email ?? ""}
```

An email-less user would get a blank handle and blank initials on the profile. It'd degrade rather than crash — the `?? ""` fallbacks hold — but it's a broken-looking profile in exchange for nothing.

- **`fitcheck-1curafus-projects.vercel.app` → 302** — a team-scoped alias that redirects. Rows 1–2.
- Rows 3–4 are wildcard patterns for **preview deployments** (`fitcheck-<hash>-1curafus-projects…`).

---
title: favicon, icon, and apple-icon
description: API Reference for the Favicon, Icon and Apple Icon file conventions.
---

The `favicon`, `icon`, or `apple-icon` file conventions allow you to set icons for your application.

They are useful for adding app icons that appear in places like web browser tabs, phone home screens, and search engine results.

There are two ways to set app icons:

- [Using image files (.ico, .jpg, .png)](#image-files-ico-jpg-png)
- [Using code to generate an icon (.js, .ts, .tsx)](#generate-icons-using-code-js-ts-tsx)

## Image files (.ico, .jpg, .png)

Use an image file to set an app icon by placing a `favicon`, `icon`, or `apple-icon` image file within your `/app` directory.
The `favicon` image can only be located in the top level of `app/`.

Next.js will evaluate the file and automatically add the appropriate tags to your app's `<head>` element.

| File convention             | Supported file types                    | Valid locations |
| --------------------------- | --------------------------------------- | --------------- |
| [`favicon`](#favicon)       | `.ico`                                  | `app/`          |
| [`icon`](#icon)             | `.ico`, `.jpg`, `.jpeg`, `.png`, `.svg` | `app/**/*`      |
| [`apple-icon`](#apple-icon) | `.jpg`, `.jpeg`, `.png`                 | `app/**/*`      |

### `favicon`

Add a `favicon.ico` image file to the root `/app` route segment.

```html filename="<head> output"
<link rel="icon" href="/favicon.ico" sizes="any" />
```

### `icon`

Add an `icon.(ico|jpg|jpeg|png|svg)` image file.

```html filename="<head> output"
<link
  rel="icon"
  href="/icon?<generated>"
  type="image/<generated>"
  sizes="<generated>"
/>
```

### `apple-icon`

Add an `apple-icon.(jpg|jpeg|png)` image file.

```html filename="<head> output"
<link
  rel="apple-touch-icon"
  href="/apple-icon?<generated>"
  type="image/<generated>"
  sizes="<generated>"
/>
```

> **Good to know**:
>
> - You can set multiple icons by adding a number suffix to the file name. For example, `icon1.png`, `icon2.png`, etc. Numbered files will sort lexically.
> - Favicons can only be set in the root `/app` segment. If you need more granularity, you can use [`icon`](#icon).
> - The appropriate `<link>` tags and attributes such as `rel`, `href`, `type`, and `sizes` are determined by the icon type and metadata of the evaluated file.
> - For example, a 32 by 32px `.png` file will have `type="image/png"` and `sizes="32x32"` attributes.
> - `sizes="any"` is added to icons when the extension is `.svg` or the image size of the file is not determined. More details in this [favicon handbook](https://evilmartians.com/chronicles/how-to-favicon-in-2021-six-files-that-fit-most-needs).

## Generate icons using code (.js, .ts, .tsx)

content.text:
Done and verified in the Simulator. All gates green — `tsc`, 844 tests, build, insights, lint at baseline.

## What landed

| | |
|---|---|
| `brand/` → `public/brand/` | its own README's `/brand/…` URLs now resolve |
| `app/favicon.ico` | ⚠️ was still the **Next.js black-N default**, live in production. Rebuilt from your 16/32/48 exports (2.3 KB vs 25 KB) |
| `app/icon.svg` · `app/apple-icon.png` | Next 16 file conventions — link tags emitted, not hand-written |
| `app/manifest.ts` | pointed at one SVG with `sizes: "any"`; now the real 192/512 rasters + maskable as its **own** entry |
| Welcome screen | the mark, 56px, above the kicker |
| `public/` | five unreferenced scaffolding SVGs deleted |

The manifest was the actual cause of the placeholder install icon: Android's installer and splash generator want real pixel sizes, and an `sizes: "any"` SVG isn't a dependable source.

## On "the logo on the whole website"

I'd push back on that one, gently. Fitcheck is a mobile PWA, not a marketing site — and apps don't repeat their logo on every screen. Where it earns its place:

- ✅ **App icon / home screen / splash** — done
